body.p: Reconsideration of the application and claims in light of the foregoing amendments and following remarks/arguments is respectfully requested. Status of the Claims
Claims 1-20 are currently pending in the present application.
In the Office Action, claims 1-20 were rejected.
The present Response amends claims 1, 5, 8-10, 12, 14, and 20 and cancels claim 4. No new matter has been added.
Upon entry of these amendments, claims 1-3 and 5-20 will be pending. Objections to the Claims
Claims 8, 9, and 20 were objected to for containing informalities. According to the
Office, the claims 8, 9, and 20 recite "CAD" without first describing the "CAD" abbreviation. See Office Action, p. 2.
As suggested by the Office, claims 8, 9, and 20 have been amended to recite "Computer-Aided Design (CAD)."
Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of objections of claims 8, 9, and 20 are respectfully requested.
The following terms in the claims of the present application were interpreted under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f):
" "robot application unit" in claim 1,
" "input interface" in claims 1, 7, and 13,
" "object data interface" in claims 1 and 9,
* "gripper finger design unit" in claims 1, 4, 5, and 8,
* "a simulation unit" in claim 10,
* "a user interface" in claim 11, and
* "a 3D view unit" in claim 12.
It is respectfully submitted that the claims 1, 4, 5, 8, 10, and 12 have now been
amended to remove reference to the phrase "unit" to avoid interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).

Further, the Applicant respectfully submits that the phrase "interface" in claims 1, 7, 9, 11, and 13, does not invoke interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f). Specifically, in order to invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), a claim limitation must, as a first prong of a three-prong analysis, use the term "means" or another nonce term. See MPEP § 2181(I). The following terms are recognized as nonce terms: "mechanism for," "module for," "device for," "unit for," "component for," "element for," "member for," "apparatus for," "machine for," or "system for." See MPEP § 2181(I)(A). In contrast, it is respectfully submitted that the phrase "interface" used in claims 1, 7, 9, 11, and 13 is not a nonce term, and would connote specific structure to a person of ordinarily skill in the art.
Thus, it is respectfully submitted that claims 1, 4-5, and 7-13 should not be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
Claims 1-20 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter.

It is respectfully submitted that the Office has not met its burden of establishing that the claims are directed to an abstract idea or that the claims do not recite significantly more. In any case, it is respectfully submitted that claims 1-20 are not directed to an abstract idea, have a practical application and contain a number of particular limitations which ensure that no underlying idea would be tied up. Additionally, it is respectfully submitted that claims 1-
20 recite features, which alone and in combination, provide improvements to computers in the technological field of robotic applications.
Applying the Office's 2019 Guidance on subject matter eligibility, it is respectfully

submitted that claims 1-20 are not directed to an abstract idea under Prong One of Step 2A of the Subject Matter Eligibility Test set forth in MPEP § 2106. Specifically, claims 1-20 are not directed to a mathematical concept, a certain method of organizing human activity, or a mental process. Rather, claims 1-20 are directed to a robot application development system.
Moreover, regardless of whether claims 1-20 are viewed as reciting an exception

under Prong One of Step 2A of the Subject Matter Eligibility Test, it is respectfully submitted that clams 1-20 provide a practical application under Prong Two of Step 2A of the Subject Matter Eligibility Test. As set forth in the 2019 Guidance, an element or combination of elements which reflect a technical improvement (e.g., to a computer or other technology) provide that a claim is directed to a practical application. In this regard, claims 1-20 recite to: determine a robot application for an industrial robot processing a work piece, wherein the robot application defines the industrial robot in a robot workspace; receive, by an input interface, robot application information characterizing the robot application; receive, by an object data interface, work piece information characterizing the work piece; and determine a gripper finger design of a gripper finger of the industrial robot, wherein the controller is configured to determine the robot application using the robot application information, wherein the controller is configured to determine the gripper finger design using the work piece information and the robot application information, and wherein the controller is configured to automatically determine a default gripper finger design using the work piece information and the robot application information. As discussed in the present application, these features provide for a robot application development system for determining a robot application for an industrial robot processing a work piece. The robot application development system is used to design a gripper finger design for a gripper finger of the industrial robot, used in the robot application. See, e.g., paragraph [0018] of the published specification (US PAP 2023/0083691 Al).
It is also respectfully submitted that the foregoing features of claims 1-20 providing the above-described technical improvements, would also provide an inventive concept under

Step 2B of the Subject Matter Eligibility Test. Moreover, claims 1-20 recite: wherein the controller is configured to automatically determine a default gripper finger design using the work piece information and the robot application information, which is not disclosed in the prior art, which also provides an inventive concept under Step 2B of the Subject Matter Eligibility Test.

For at least the foregoing reasons, it is respectfully submitted that claims 1-20 are directed to patent-eligible subject matter pursuant to the 2019 Guidance. Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 is respectfully requested.
Claims 1-3, 5-12, 14-16, and 18-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as being
anticipated by US Wolniakowski et al., "Task and Context Sensitive Gripper Design Learning Using Dynamic Grasp Simulation" ("Wolniakowski").
Claims 4, 13, and 17 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Wolniakowski and further in view of Corkum et al., US 2020/0398492 Al ("Corkum").

Independent claim 1 of the present application has now been amended to incorporate the subject matter of claim 4 to recite "wherein the controller is configured to automatically determine a default gripper finger design using the work piece information and the robot application information."
Support for the amendments can be found, for example, in paragraphs [0039] of the published specification.1
It is respectfully submitted that Wolniakowski and Corkum, alone or in combination, fail to disclose or suggest the foregoing features of amended claim 1.
In rejecting previously pending claim 4, the Office correctly concedes that
Wolniakowski does not disclose "automatically determining a default gripper finger design

using the work piece information and the robot application information," but states that Corkum teaches this subject matter at paragraph [0069]. See Office Action, p. 18. Applicant respectfully disagrees because the cited portion of Corkum simply discloses queuing a validated design for printing at a 3D printer or other additive manufacturing system.

Corkum describes autonomously generating an end effector for interfacing with a part at a manufacturing station. See Corkum, Abstract. The cited portion of Corkum is only related to production and deployment. The cited portion of Corkum simply teaches that the computer system can queue the manufacture of an end effector according to a virtual 3D end effector model, once the computer system has generated and validated the virtual 3D end effector model. See Corkum, paragraph [0069]. However, the cited portion of Corkum is completely silent regarding how the virtual 3D end effector is generated or validated. At best, the cited portion of Corkum simply provides a validated design for printing at a 3D printer or other additive manufacturing system.
Therefore, Corkum does not show or suggest "determining a default gripper finger design using the work piece information and the robot application information," as recited in amended claim 1.

Because the combination of Wolniakowski and Corkum fails to disclose or suggest at least the above-recited features of amended independent claim 1, the combination of Wolniakowski and Corkum cannot anticipate or render obvious claim 1 or any of its dependent claims 2-3 and 5-13 obvious.

Regarding independent claim 14, while amended independent claim 14 differs from amended independent claim 1 in overall claim scope, amended claim 14 recites substantially similar features as amended claim 1 and were rejected for substantially similar reasons as claim 1. Accordingly, for similar reasons as discussed above, Wolniakowski and Corkum fail to anticipate or render obvious all of the features of amended independent claim 14 and its dependent claims 15-20.
Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection of claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 based on Wolniakowski in combination with Corkum is respectfully requested.

Applicant believes that all issues raised by the Office have been addressed and that the present application is allowable for the foregoing reasons. If there are any remaining issues which the Office believes could be resolved through either a Supplemental Response or an Examiner's Amendment, Applicant respectfully invites the Office to call the telephone contact at the number indicated below.
